# Fortran Indentation and Declaration Rules
- Use spaces for indentation and alignment; do not use tab characters in Fortran source files.
- Separate every `implicit none` statement from surrounding code with a blank line immediately before and immediately after it, including when it follows a module or procedure header directly.
- Place a blank line immediately before every `end subroutine` statement, separating it from the preceding code or comment.
- In intrinsic `integer`, `real`, `complex`, and `logical` declarations, use positional kind selectors without `kind=`, for example `integer(i_def)` and `real(r_def)`, not `integer(kind=i_def)` or `real(kind=r_def)`. Preserve the existing kind expression; omit only the keyword, not the selector. Do not apply this rewrite to `character`: `character(str_def)` selects length, not kind, so retain an explicit `kind=` when a character kind is specified. This rule concerns datatype declarations, not kind arguments in intrinsic procedure calls or parameters of derived types.
- Write real-valued numeric literals with at least one digit after the decimal point, for example `1.0` rather than `1.` and `1.0e3` rather than `1e3`, so they are clearly distinguished from integer literals.
- For Fortran source lines, aim for 80 columns and allow up to 85 when needed for readable wrapping or alignment. Shorter lines are fine; do not pad them.
- Apply the symmetric interior-spacing rule to matched delimiters enclosing grouped expressions, procedure argument lists, and constructor elements, except for square-bracket and legacy `(/ ... /)` array constructors in a vertically aligned multi-line group; use the array-alignment rule below for those constructors.
- In procedure calls with named arguments, write `name=value` with no spaces around `=`. Separate arguments on the same line with a comma followed by exactly one space: `arg1, arg2`.
- Use one space after commas in ordinary lists. When aligning positional arguments across a vertically aligned multi-line argument group, pad after commas as needed to align corresponding argument starts. For an outer array-constructor separator before a trailing continuation marker, keep exactly one space between the comma and `&`, for example: `item, &`.
- Format counted `do` loops as `do i=<start>, <end>[, <stride>]`, with one space after each comma. Parentheses around bounds are optional unless needed to express the intended arithmetic. Omit `<stride>` only when the default increment of 1 is intended, for example: `do i=0, nlayers-1`.
- For dummy arguments of `function_space_type`, `global_mesh_type`, `halo_routing_type`, `local_mesh_type`, or `mesh_type` declared `intent(in)`, omit the `pointer` attribute. These long-lived LFRic objects are passed as data; their dummy pointer association is not part of the procedure interface. After removing the attribute, recompute the shared columns of adjacent declarations (especially `intent` and `::`): preserve clear alignment using the updated declarations, but remove padding needed only to retain columns from before the removal.
- Within a file, use the `only:` or `only :` spelling that occurs in the majority of its `use` statements. If the counts are tied, or the file has no existing `only` clauses, use `only:`. Keep continued imported names aligned when changing the spelling.
- In a contiguous block of `use` statements at the same indentation level, align all `only:` (or `only :`) clauses in one column, with exactly one space after the comma following the longest module name. Pad after the commas of shorter module names to reach that column. This overrides the ordinary single-space-after-comma rule for this alignment padding only. Align continued imported names under the first imported name after the `only` clause, with exactly one space after the colon. Recompute the alignment for the whole block when module names change, and verify clause and continuation columns with a non-compiling check.

```fortran
use argument_mod,  only: arg_type, GH_FIELD, GH_REAL, GH_INC, GH_READ, &
                         ANY_SPACE_1, CELL_COLUMN
use constants_mod, only: i_def, r_def
use kernel_mod,    only: kernel_type
```

- When normalising delimiter spacing in a vertically aligned group of statements, preserve the original columns of corresponding tokens on adjacent lines. Move compensating whitespace outside the delimiters rather than changing the required symmetric interior spacing, and verify the columns against the pre-edit layout.
- For square-bracket (`[ ... ]`) and legacy (`(/ ... /)`) array constructors in a vertically aligned multi-line group, keep each opening delimiter (`[` or `(/`) in the same column and align corresponding element fields vertically, padding each position to the width of its widest element. This takes precedence over symmetric and zero-or-one-space delimiter rules: opening-side padding may vary by row and differ from the closing-side gap; keep one space before each closing delimiter (`]` or `/)`). Do not shift the opening delimiter to compensate. Preserve the non-whitespace token sequence and verify delimiter, element, and comma columns across the complete group. Do not apply this exception to array subscripts or ordinary procedure argument lists.
- For spacing-only edits, compare the pre-edit and post-edit code with whitespace ignored; the non-whitespace token sequence must be unchanged. Inspect the full affected construct and diff to ensure no statement was accidentally added, removed, or moved.
- Before bulk spacing edits to procedure arguments, use a Fortran-aware parser to confirm each comma or delimiter belongs to an actual argument list; punctuation alone is not sufficient. Do not classify array constructors, array sections/subscripts, or text inside strings/comments as procedure arguments. If parsing fails or the source mapping is ambiguous, use a fallback only after checking it against representative parsed cases; otherwise skip and report the location.
- **Copyright required:** Every new or edited LFRic source file must contain a copyright notice. Inspect the complete header, recognising forms including `(C) Crown copyright` and `Copyright (c) YEAR, Met Office`; do not rely on one literal phrase. Preserve existing copyright text and years. If a notice is absent, insert the default LFRic project notice below. This default has no year; do not add one. Before completing the task, verify that each new or edited source file has its copyright notice before AI attribution and documentation.
- **Default LFRic project copyright notice:** Use the following wording exactly, adapting only the comment syntax to the source language (for example, `!` for Fortran, `#` for Python, or `//` for C-like languages). For languages requiring block comments, enclose the same notice text and dividers in valid comment delimiters.

	```fortran
	!-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
	! (c) Crown copyright Met Office. All rights reserved.
	! The file LICENCE, distributed with this code, contains details of the terms
	! under which the code may be used.
	!-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
	```

- **AI attribution:** Place attribution immediately after the complete copyright block's closing divider and before existing documentation. Do not add AI attribution to XML or JSON files. Do not infer the institution name, AI tool, model version, or PR numbers from existing repository files or attributions; use only values confirmed for the current change. If any value is unavailable, ask rather than guessing or copying it from another file. AI attribution is not a substitute for the required copyright notice. If the notice is missing, follow the copyright rule above; do not treat attribution at file start as satisfying the header requirements.

- Apply LFRic Doxygen markup to interface and algorithm-layer code. Give every program unit in scope and every public API entity a one-line `@brief`; add `@details` where useful. Describe every user-supplied procedure argument with `@param`, including intent and name, and document function results with `@return`. Omit implicit passed-object dummies from type-bound procedure parameter lists, as detailed below. Public API entities include public types, parameters, variables, and procedures, including procedures exposed through type-bound bindings. Document a type-bound procedure where its implementing function or subroutine is written. The type-bound reference in the derived-type definition does not require its own Doxygen block or a duplicate `@brief`; do not flag its absence during review when the implementation is documented. Follow the project exclusions: do not Doxygen standalone `program` blocks, tests, or PSykal-light code. Use ordinary comments for private members. When the program-unit requirement applies to a non-public procedure, document it as internal developer documentation, not public API documentation.
- Determine the passed-object dummy from the type-bound binding declaration, not its name. If `PASS(name)` is specified, that named dummy is the passed object; if `PASS` is omitted, the first procedure dummy is passed unless the binding is `NOPASS`. Omit the passed-object dummy from the Doxygen `@param` block regardless of its name, because callers supply it through the object, not as a separate argument. Document all other user-supplied arguments. For an ordinary procedure call, document every explicit argument, including an object argument. When changing the `@param` block, recompute argument-name and description columns for the whole block using the rightmost `]` and longest argument name. Before accepting a type-bound Doxygen block, compare its parameter list with the binding and procedure dummies: verify the passed-object dummy is absent and every other explicit dummy appears exactly once.
- Indent a procedure's leading Doxygen block exactly like its procedure statement. Do not apply a separate fixed Doxygen indent; preserve the shared indentation on every comment and continuation line.
- Determine `@param` direction from user-visible data flow, not only the dummy argument's Fortran `intent`. Trace writes through pointer components, pointer targets, aliases, and relevant callees. For a dummy declared `intent(in)` whose reachable target data is modified, describe that mutation explicitly and use `@param[in,out]` to reflect the effective data mutation; do not imply that the dummy's pointer association changes unless it does.
- For procedure Doxygen comments, when a block has only one description directive (`@brief` or `@details`), use exactly one space between the directive and its text. When both are present, align their description text to the same column. Within each `@param` block, align argument names so each begins exactly one space after the block's rightmost closing bracket `]`; pad after shorter direction tags as needed. Align descriptions within each block to one column: use exactly two spaces after the longest argument name, and pad after shorter names so their descriptions start in that same column. Use only Doxygen direction values `[in]`, `[out]`, and `[in,out]`; do not put Fortran's `optional` attribute in the direction brackets. For an argument declared `optional`, begin its `@param` description with `Optional: `. If an `@param` description wraps, align each continuation line with the first character of that description.
- For wrapped `@brief` and `@details` descriptions, align each continuation line with the first character of the description text, not with the directive name.
- Treat each complete `@param` block as one alignment group, including mixed direction tags and generated support arguments. For each description, calculate the space gap as `(longest argument-name length - current argument-name length) + 2`. Recompute the whole block after adding, removing, or renaming any argument; do not copy existing padding or estimate visually. Before accepting the edit, use a non-compiling column check to verify that all argument names start in one column, all descriptions start in one column, and the longest name has exactly two spaces after it. Check wrapped description lines against that same description column.

	Correct alignment (`increment` has 9 characters, so `nlayers` needs 4 spaces before its description, not 3):

	```fortran
	!! @param[in]     nlayers    Number of vertical layers.
	!! @param[in,out] increment  Field receiving source contributions.
	!! @param[in]     source     Values added to the increment field.
	!! @param[in]     ndf        Degrees of freedom per column.
	!! @param[in]     undf       Unique degrees of freedom in the function space.
	!! @param[in]     map        Dof map for the current column.
	```
- Format a function return as `@return <result_name>  <description>`, with exactly two spaces between the result name and description. Use the explicit `RESULT` variable when present, otherwise the function name. Do not align the return description with other directives.
- Write `@param` descriptions as concise noun phrases, telegraphic phrases, or fragments rather than full sentences. Describe the argument without imperative wording.
- Do not begin `@param` or `@return` descriptions with the articles `a`, `an`, or `the`. When reviewing existing comments, flag such descriptions for removal and call them out to the user; remove the leading article when editing.
- Aim to keep reflowed Doxygen comment text within 80 columns, but treat this as guidance rather than a hard limit. Reflow paragraphs to avoid leaving an isolated word on the final line; extend the right edge to column 83 when needed to keep the text block readable and balanced.
- For a newly created Doxygen block, add this uppercase warning as Doxygen comments so it appears in generated documentation. Align the `!!` continuation text with the text after `@note`, then include an empty `!>` line before `@brief`. Do not add or restore the note on an existing Doxygen block where it is absent; treat its absence as intentional developer review. If the note is present, keep it until a developer has reviewed the documentation for correctness, then remove it:

	```fortran
	!> @note THESE COMMENTS WERE ADDED BY AI AND MUST BE REVIEWED FOR CORRECTNESS.
	!!       REMOVE THIS COMMENT AFTER DEVELOPER REVIEW.
	!>
	```
- In module-contained procedures, keep the leading documentation, procedure statement, and matching `end function` or `end subroutine` in column 1. Indent declarations, executable statements, and standalone procedure-body comments two spaces. Increase indentation by two spaces for each nested construct and align each terminator with its opener. Treat module-level `contains` as a scope separator, not a nesting level; derive indentation from construct nesting, not existing whitespace. Within a derived-type definition, align its `contains` statement with the opening `type` statement and matching `end type`; treat it as opening the type-binding section, with all bindings and their associated or standalone comments indented two spaces beyond `contains`. In `select case` and `select type`, align labels with the selector and indent each branch's immediate contents two spaces beyond its label.
- Associate a contiguous leading comment block with a module-contained procedure when it documents the procedure or its arguments. This includes plain `!` comments and Doxygen comments (`!>`, `!!`), even if one blank line separates the block from the procedure statement. Align the complete block, including all comment lines and blank documentation lines, with the procedure statement. Keep both in column 1 when the statement is in column 1. Do not apply this rule to type or component documentation.
- In `.pf` unit tests, align each procedure header decorator (for example, `@test`) with the associated `function` or `subroutine` statement.
- For pFUnit unit-test tasks (`*.pf` files), load `.github/skills/lfric-unit-test/SKILL.md` for test design, fixtures, assertions, kernel inputs, and validation guidance.
- In a function or subroutine statement with at least one argument on the same line as `(`, allow no more than one blank space between `(` and the first argument. For continued procedure headers, align continuation arguments under that first argument and preserve trailing `&` marker columns. For matched `()`, `[]`, or `{}` delimiters enclosing procedure arguments or constructor elements, use zero or one symmetric interior space except for square-bracket and legacy `(/ ... /)` array constructors in vertically aligned multi-line groups; those follow the array-alignment rule above. This concerns spacing inside delimiters, not between a procedure name and `(`.
- For a continued `call` statement with at least one argument on its first line, put no space between the procedure name and `(`, and indent each continuation line to the first argument's column. After applying other formatting rules, if a continued statement has exactly one trailing `&`, put exactly one space before it. If it has multiple trailing markers, use one style consistently throughout the statement: either align all markers in one column or put exactly one space before each marker. If existing markers follow neither style, use the aligned-column style. Choose a shared marker column beyond the rightmost code token, preserving any required separator whitespace before `&` (for example, the single space in `item, &`). Adjust only padding before the markers; do not remove required separators to force alignment.
- For continuation lines supplying arguments or array-constructor values to a named function or subroutine, indent the first nonblank character at least four columns beyond the function or subroutine name's starting column. Align an array constructor's closing `]` with its continuation values. When aligning operands, change only leading indentation; when applying the selected trailing-`&` style, change only padding immediately before the markers. Do not alter non-whitespace tokens. Check that all marker tokens remain present and line lengths remain valid.
- For continued assignment statements, align hanging right-hand-side expression operands with the first nonblank character after the assignment `=` wherever line-length limits permit. This applies to expression continuations, not nested procedure argument lists or array constructors, which retain their own alignment rules. Change only leading indentation; preserve non-whitespace tokens and continuation markers. Verify operand columns across the complete continued statement.
- Keep every declaration and specification statement in a procedure before its first executable statement. When moving an initialization out of a declaration, place the executable initialization only after the final declaration; never leave declarations after it.
- Declare one data entity per declaration statement, with each declaration starting on its own line, except for local loop counters as described below. Split other comma-separated entity lists into separate declarations, repeating the applicable datatype and attributes. An array is one entity; do not split its dimensions or constructor elements. Preserve entity order, initialisation, kinds, shapes, intents, and all other attributes.
- Local loop counters may share a declaration when their datatype, kind, and attributes are identical. Precede the local-loop-counter declaration block immediately with the ordinary comment `! Local loop counters`, indented to match the declarations. Do not combine loop counters with dummy arguments or other local variables.
- Keep dummy-argument declarations and local-variable declarations in separate groups, with a blank line between them. Place all dummy-argument declarations before the local-variable declarations. Each group may contain multiple blank-line-separated alignment blocks. Do not mix declarations with `intent(...)` and local-variable declarations in the same block or continued declaration statement. Identify dummy arguments from the procedure interface, not solely from the presence of `intent`, so arguments without an explicit `intent` remain in the argument group. Preserve all declaration attributes and keep both groups before executable statements.
- Where line-length limits permit, order declaration attributes consistently within each contiguous declaration block so corresponding fields align clearly. For dummy arguments, place `intent(...)` before `dimension(...)`; align `intent`, `dimension` where present, and `::` in shared columns by padding between fields. Keep exactly one space after `::`. Declarations without a corresponding attribute leave that field empty rather than adding an attribute. If alignment would require more than five consecutive spaces between declaration fields, start a new block separated by a blank line and recompute alignment independently for each block; do not count leading indentation towards this limit. Preserve variable order, kinds, shapes, intents, and all other attributes; do not move declarations across dependency or argument/local-group boundaries merely for alignment. Recompute columns for each block after changes and verify them with a non-compiling check. Attribute reordering and entity-list splitting are not whitespace-only edits: verify each entity retains the same attributes and is declared exactly once.
- Before adding `nullify(pointer)` for a procedure-local pointer, trace its first use on every reachable path. If a direct pointer-association assignment (`=>`) occurs before every use, do not add entry nullification. Otherwise, place `nullify` after all declarations and before any possible use.
- Do not automatically compile or build Fortran code. Use static diagnostics and non-compiling checks by default; compile or build only when explicitly requested by the user.
- After changing declaration-time initialization, check the full procedure for declaration ordering and use the narrowest available non-compiling validation.

# LFRic Kernel Rules
- For kernel tasks, load `.github/skills/lfric-kernel/SKILL.md`. Within repository guidance, explicit kernel-specific rules in that skill take precedence over conflicting general Fortran rules for kernel code; all non-conflicting general rules remain in force.
- Place kernel modules under the owning application's or component's `source/kernel` directory, following the neighbouring source-file extension and naming conventions.
- Declare kernel metadata in a public type extending `kernel_type`. Keep `meta_args` in the order expected by the code procedure, set `operates_on` to the intended iteration space, and bind the code procedure with `nopass`.
- Within a vertically aligned `meta_args` constructor, align corresponding positional arguments across adjacent `arg_type` elements with padding after commas as needed. Keep outer constructor separators and continuation markers aligned, retaining one space in `, &`.
- Add an inline comment to each `meta_args` element naming its corresponding user-supplied argument dummy in the kernel code procedure. Keep the names in metadata and procedure-argument order. For continued elements, put the comment after the continuation marker and preserve required comma spacing, for example: `arg_type(...), & ! temperature`.
- In a kernel metadata type, indent every component declaration exactly two spaces beyond the opening `type` statement. Keep `meta_args` aligned with sibling components, and verify component indentation independently from constructor continuation operands, closing delimiters, and `&` marker columns.
- Keep metadata and implementation interfaces consistent: each kernel argument's access mode, datatype, function space, and stencil or operator properties must agree with the code and its dummy arguments. Set each data dummy's `intent` to reflect that access.
- Do not access runtime source data through variables imported with `use`; pass those values through kernel metadata and code-procedure arguments. Use-associated variables in a kernel must be named constants declared with the Fortran `parameter` attribute.
- Derive the complete code-procedure dummy list from the LFRic/PSyclone kernel interface for the metadata. Include required generated arguments such as layer counts, dof counts, dofmaps, stencil sizes and maps, and operator or quadrature data. For non-trivial metadata, check a comparable kernel or generated interface rather than guessing the argument order.
- Index field data through the supplied dofmaps and dimensions, and iterate only over the valid degrees of freedom and layers for the selected function space and iteration space. Do not assume a single degree of freedom or access stencil entries beyond the supplied stencil size unless the metadata guarantees it.
- Limit writes to arguments declared writable by the metadata; avoid hidden state changes and I/O in kernel code.
